Hex houses

One L-shaped house at all twelve 30° angles on one empty terrain, with the hex grid showing. The house is its cells; the walls follow from them (WORLD.md § One game, square or hex).

  • terrain cells
  • the house's cells
  • the thin walls the rules use: the edges between inside and outside
  • a tops wall: the wobble across the tops of a row of hexes
  • a sides wall: along the sides of hexes under each other
  • a wall off the house's axes (none should be)

Even angles are the grid's own edge directions, odd angles its corner directions: a 30° turn is no symmetry of the hex grid, so the two families give different cells. A house's two axes are always one of each, so every house has both kinds of straight wall. Each is solved from the wall edges alone (hexhouse::solve_tops, solve_sides): turned to its own frame, the line runs through the midpoints its pattern puts on it (every edge across the tops; every slanted connector along the sides), along the wall's heading exactly, mitred where two walls meet.

Turning: the 0° house is the plan's cells. 60°, 120°, … are that house turned cell for cell (a 60° turn is a symmetry of the grid). 30° cannot be a copy, so each room is its rectangle turned 30° and grown or shrunk evenly until it holds as many cells as at 0°, or the nearest whole rows come to that; 90°, 150°, … are the 30° house turned cell for cell. Here the body keeps its 19 cells at every angle and the side room has 18 at 0° and 16 at 30°.

Any shape, any angle: walls from the cells alone

The hex and wall model knows no angle. A house is its cells; the thin walls are the edges between inside and outside; the straight walls are solved from those edges. Even the axes the walls run along are read off the cells (hexhouse::axes_of: each boundary edge votes for the heading nearest the way the boundary travels). What matters is that every hex centre is clearly inside or outside: on every house here none is on the wrong side of the drawn walls, and none lies under a wall.

The 2 × 2 box (3 × 3 m) is the same seven cells, one hex and its six neighbours, at every angle: its cells show no direction, the vote ties, and only then does the angle it was placed at decide. It marks the limit: a structure must be big enough for its cells to carry its walls, and anything smaller (an outhouse, a well) is a special object with its own rotation instead.
